title: Type widening, narrowing, and control flow
hook: TypeScript starts with a precise type and sometimes broadens it on purpose — or narrows it when your `if` checks prove which branch you are in. Understanding both directions keeps your unions useful instead of accidentally turning into plain `string`.

blocks.text: **Widening** is when TypeScript infers a broader type than the literal you wrote — `let x = "hello"` becomes `string`, not `"hello"`. **Narrowing** is the opposite: after a type guard (`typeof`, `===`, `in`, `instanceof`), the compiler refines a union to a specific member. **Control-flow analysis** tracks narrowing across `if`, `else`, `switch`, early returns, and assignment checks. The `as const` assertion freezes literals and prevents widening. C# has definite assignment and pattern narrowing; TypeScript's version is entirely compile-time on erased types.

entries.plainDefinition: When a literal type (like "pending") is inferred as a wider type (like string) because the variable could be reassigned.
When control flow proves a more specific type, the compiler updates the variable's type in that branch.
Tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest readonly literal types and prevent widening on objects and arrays.
entries.example: `const roles = ["admin", "user"] as const;` → readonly tuple of literals.

blocks.text: Widening is why your exhaustive `switch` suddenly accepts any `string`. Narrowing is why TypeScript catches missing null checks before production. Senior engineers pair **`unknown` at boundaries** with narrowing guards — the top Reddit/LeetCode pattern for safe parsing. Without narrowing discipline, unions degrade to `any`-like behavior through assertions.

blocks.title: const vs let
blocks.body: `const x = "a"` keeps the literal type `"a"` because reassignment is impossible. `let x = "a"` widens to `string` because you might assign another string later.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Narrow with guards
items.body: Equality, `typeof`, `in`, `instanceof`, and user-defined type predicates refine unions inside branches.

diagram.title: Control-flow narrowing
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  START["value: string | null"] --> CHECK{"=== null?"}
  CHECK -->|yes| NULL["branch: null"]
  CHECK -->|no| STR["branch: string"]
  NULL --> EARLY["early return"]
  STR --> USE["safe string ops"]

snippet.label: Widening with let vs const
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `const` preserves the literal because the binding never changes. Line 2: `let` widens to `string` — the compiler assumes reassignment. Lines 5–6: assigning a union member to `string` is fine; assigning to a const literal type is not.

snippet.label: as const prevents widening
snippet.explanation: Line 4: `as const` makes properties readonly literal types. Line 6: indexing the const object yields a union of literals. Line 12: passing `HTTP.GET` stays typed as `"GET"`, not widened `string`.

snippet.label: Control-flow narrowing guards
snippet.explanation: Line 2: union of three types. Lines 3–5: null check removes `null` from the union. Lines 6–8: typeof removes `string`. Line 10: only `number` remains — no assertion needed.

snippet.label: Failure mode — assertion instead of narrowing
snippet.explanation: Line 3: `as string` on `unknown` compiles but throws at runtime for wrong shapes. Lines 5–8: throw narrows `unknown` to `string` in the success path — the production-safe pattern for API boundaries.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `let` for fixed literal unions and losing exhaustiveness. Asserting `as` instead of narrowing `unknown`. Assuming narrowing survives across function boundaries — it does not unless you use a type predicate (module 11).

blocks.text: Widening applies to `null` and `undefined` in non-strictNullChecks legacy code — always enable strict null. **Discriminated unions** narrow on a shared literal field (next topic). Type predicates (`function isFish(x): x is Fish`) extend narrowing across call sites. Assignment narrowing (`if (x = maybeString)`) works but is easy to confuse with comparison — prefer `===`. Control-flow analysis does not cross async gaps without manual annotation — after `await`, re-narrow if the value could change.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Must be honest — lying breaks trust

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Not knowing why let widens and const does not. Using as on unknown in production paths. Claiming narrowing persists after await without re-check. Confusing widening with type coercion at runtime.

interviewTakeaways: `let` widens literals to base types; `const` and `as const` preserve literals.
Narrowing follows control flow — if, else, switch, throw, and early return.
Use `unknown` at API boundaries and narrow; never trust `as` alone.
typeof, ===, in, and instanceof are built-in narrowing guards.
60s: Widening makes types broader on mutable bindings. Narrowing refines unions after checks. as const freezes literals. C# uses patterns; TS uses flow analysis on erased types.
commonPitfalls: let status = "pending" widens to string — breaks literal exhaustiveness.
Asserting unknown to a concrete type without validation.
Strong answer: 'const keeps literals. Guards narrow unions. unknown + narrow at boundaries. Widening is compile-time inference, not JS coercion.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Narrowing guards map directly to JavaScript runtime checks. TypeScript adds compile-time proof that the right checks exist.
C# `if (x is string s)` is the closest analog. TypeScript has more guard forms but no run-time type reification.
